Everyone would love to get their hands on some magic pill which solves all your problems while you have a nap or chill out. Losing 10kg overnight, earning a million bucks in a week, gaining experience by watching YouTube videos... whatever. Such "magic pills" don't exist, and most problems require some sort of effort to solve them. The only variable is how much effort is required.

Just like life itself... relationships, careers, and watch collecting all have a proven easier way to solve things or a hard way. The trick, of course, is to find the 'proven easier way'. What does that mean? Well, you've got to find the person who has already solved the problem that you’re facing for the first time.

As google will reveal - nearly every problem you face today, has been faced previously by someone, somewhere. You've just got to find them. This is probably why successful people have a larger and more varied network of relationships in their lives than less successful ones. The same holds true for watch collectors too.

If you think about your career for a second... Earlier in your career, what you know tends to matter a bit more than who you know. As you progress, however, who you know increasingly dictates your overall success. Why is that? I would argue that when you align yourself with high performing, diverse, and interesting people, you discover two key things. First , these people bring to your attention things like novel ideas, tools, and skills... and these things give you a competitive advantage in your career. Second , and this is by definition of course, these same people tend to connect you with other high-performing, diverse, and interesting people. This is a perpetual loop.

The same, I have found, is true for watch collecting. There are many watch collectors out there who have been collecting for several decades, and have seen and experienced countless watches over the years. Particularly in today's hype market, this fact is more relevant now than ever before... because these more experienced collectors have had the privilege of experiencing the watches without all the associated 'noise' that comes with hype. They have a perspective which many will fail to gain through experience today.

With that in mind, I suggest that there are two kinds of relationships for budding collectors to form, nurture, and maintain:

PEERS - Like minded peers with whom you share a similar approach to collecting, be it from a brand values perspective, budget, or any other area of common ground. More importantly, find people who are at a similar stage of collecting as yourself, Form an alliance with them. Help them. Ask them to help you. Work as a team. Together, you all get ahead further and faster than any one of you alone. A strong, diverse team beats the lone individual every time. This applies in the workplace, and it applies in collecting too. Rather than trying to compete with one another, you can help one another find the things you're searching for, advise one another, and share your own experiences regarding certain watches. Think of it like a 'collective brain' of like-minded enthusiasts.

MENTORS - These are the people who are further ahead of you in their collecting journey, from whom you want to learn. Seek out a more experienced collector whose collection seems to appeal to you the most... be it in terms of aesthetics, historical significance, craftsmanship or whatever other characteristics appeal to you the most. Get to know that person (or people). Learn from them. You can even ask that person to be a formal mentor, although most folks are wary of making formal commitments... It's probably better to develop the relationship informally. Observe from a distance to start, then maybe connect over a zoom call, a coffee or lunch... Ask them questions about themselves, their collecting journey, and in particular, ask for advice they would share with a younger version of themselves.

My own advice on dealing with these people is limited, and I'm sure you will all have your own approach... I would ensure that your gratitude is unequivocal... Thank them a lot... remain mindful that they are probably super busy and their time is both valuable and limited. What I believe is the more you are highly respectful of people's time, the more they are willing to help. If you act as though you are somehow entitled to their time, they feel disrespected and try to distance themselves from you.

In the end, a good teacher teaches you what you want to know, but a good mentor exposes you to ideas that you need to know... even if you don’t realise it yet.

-F

I had a funny exchange at the gym several months ago, and I’ve been wanting to write about it for a while… This week’s SDC Weekly is nearly done but I have some updates to add from Geneva Watch Days; I decided to delay it to later this week, and share this story today instead.

There’s a guy at my gym who I’ve known for over ten years, and like most ‘gym-friends’ I have ever had, I still don’t know his name. I think his nickname is “T”, he’s mid-fifties, works part-time as a PT, and for someone his age he is, admittedly, in decent shape. None of that is super-important to the story, but I figured it was worth setting the scene.

What you do need to know is that this guy wears a five-digit Rolex Sea-Dweller and I have never seen him without it. I remember asking him about it many years ago, and he told me he bought it ages before that, and only ever takes it off when he goes to bed. Now to be clear, he’s emphatically not a watch guy. He bought it because it’s a Rolex, and by his own admission he is very much a “hype guy” (his words) - he’s always rocking the latest trainers, latest phone, latest AirPods… he enjoys spending money on whatever conspicuous consumables he can afford (again, his words, not my own psychoanalysis).

Anyway, we got chatting about watches one day and I made the mistake of getting a bit carried away. I started telling him about the titanium Yacht-Master and I pulled out my phone to show him a photo of the matte bezel. As I was speaking, I said something like “this bezel is ceramic, and yours is aluminium.”

He got visibly irate instantly... “No, no, mine is ceramic.”

At first I thought he was winding me up so I tried again. I told him I’d owned the exact reference he’s wearing, that it’s a five-digit Sea-Dweller, and that Rolex didn’t even use ceramic on the Sea-Dweller until the 116600 came out with the Cerachrom insert. I explained how, before that, every Sea-Dweller had an aluminium bezel. In my mind, this is not even a controversial claim; anyone can verify this in about 10 seconds on the internet.

But no… his eyes grew wide and his voice was a tad aggressive. “I think I’d know my watch better than you.”

Somehow I couldn’t bring myself to stop there (I should have, but ego is a ghastly thing); I pointed to the scratches on his (well-worn) bezel and said “ ceramic doesn’t wear like that .” To be honest, I wasn’t trying to be a d1ck about it (though I’m sure the astonishment on my face might have read as sarcasm). I tried to soften it by saying something like “ aluminium isn’t a bad thing, it’s just that Rolex didn’t introduce ceramic bezels until later” - I don’t remember my exact words but you get the idea.

And he goes, flatly, “Ok, whatever you say” - again, with super-defiant, wide eyes. So I rolled my eyes and walked away, reminding myself that I am not the fvckface whisperer .

This guy still doesn’t talk to me… it’s been several months now!

—

As I proceeded to complete my next set, the penny dropped for me. What he said, is exactly what I should have said from the start: “ Ok, whatever you say. ” The second I realised he believed (like, truly believed) that his bezel was ceramic, I should have just dropped it, because nothing I was going to say in the next five minutes was going to change anything except how much he hated me for implying his prized possession was ‘inferior’ to what he believed it was (even though that wasn’t my intention at all ).

Discomfort

Obviously, being wrong about the bezel material on your watch is no big deal, but what I was blown away by was how certain this guy was. He was deeply, unshakeably, and even emotionally… certain . Not “I think it might be ceramic” and more like “I know I’m right and you’re a weapons-grade moron for suggesting otherwise.”

This is true despite the fact that the receipts on my side were pretty overwhelming. I told him I owned the same watch, I pointed out the scratches on his own bezel… none of that stuff entered his head.

As I said, I’ve ‘known’ this guy for over a decade, and we’ve spoken many times in the gym, and used to exchange pleasantries daily. I don’t think he’s completely stupid, so presumably, from his side, he was just as sure that I was the confused one in this exchange. Which means he probably went home thinking “that idiot at the gym tried to tell me my Rolex is aluminium” with exactly the same conviction I went home thinking the opposite.

Where I ended up after this exchange was to consider how, if this can happen over something as trivial (and verifiable) as a bezel’s material, this goes to show how easily it can happen about anything else. So I was wondering, how many things do I “ know I know” that are actually just things I happen to believe , but which have somehow calcified through repetition into a ‘ feeling of fact ’?

People are much better at changing their minds when they don’t have to admit they were wrong, to do so.

As one does, I went looking for what the research says, and boy oh boy, it’s not flattering at all…

Research about being wrong and not knowing it

The earliest useful work in this area is a 1975 study by Lee Ross, Mark Lepper and Mary Hubbard at Stanford. 1 In this study, they gave people a task which seemed serious, but was all made up (they had to filter out real suicide notes from made-up ones).

After they had completed the task, participants were randomly told whether they had done well or badly. Once everyone had received feedback, the researchers then debriefed participants and told them all feedback was BS, and that their assigned scores were random.

Somehow, the participants still rated themselves according to the fake feedback; so those who had been told they did well continued to think they were good at the task, and those who had been told they did badly continued to think they were bad at it.

Even after they were explicitly told that the evidence was BS, the belief they had based on the initial evidence still stuck around in their heads. 2 Ross and his collaborators called this belief perseverance , and just for your info, this effect has in fact been replicated in dozens of studies since.

One particular follow-up study by Craig Anderson, Lepper and Ross in 1980 offered a little insight into why the beliefs stick. Once you’ve formed a belief, you build a little causal story in your head to explain why it’s true. And once the causal story exists, it becomes independent of the evidence that originally produced it. You can take the evidence away entirely and the story will carry on running by itself, because it becomes the new foundation. 3

Translating that into my gym situation, my guy might seem to just own a Rolex with an aluminium bezel, but in his head, he has a whole personal narrative around it. Rolex is unbeatable to him, and he knows ‘he bought the best’. He has worn it every day for many years, and so of course it’s ceramic, because of course the best-in-class brand he chose would have put the best-in-class material on the best-in-class watch. To him that’s what feels correct and satisfies the emotional narrative in his head, and so, whatever I do will just end up bouncing off the narrative he’s got in his head.

There’s this study by Lord, Ross and Lepper which analysed peoples’ attitudes toward capital punishment. For both people who favoured or didn’t favour the death penalty, they showed a mixed bag of studies (for and against) and then asked them to evaluate the research. Of course, you already know what happened… if a study supported their own views, it was ‘more rigorous’ and if it didn’t, it was ‘more flawed’ . The point being, the exact same data made a group of people who didn’t agree, become more convinced of their original position than when they started! Just so you know the term and I can refer back to it someday, the researchers called this biased assimilation . 4

What I find mind-blowing is that even if we are presented with contrary evidence, it seems we process it, and then come out the other side feeling more confident in the view we started with. The gym guy’s scratched bezel, which to me was ‘exhibit A’, was probably ‘exhibit A’ for him, too!

Going further, we also have Leon Festinger’s original cognitive dissonance work from the 1950s . You probably know this theory already; holding two incompatible ideas in your head makes you physically uncomfortable, and therefore you’ll do almost anything to fix this discomfort. This might even include changing what you believe about the world, just to fit something you have already done 5 . If you think about it, it tends to be much easier for people to change a belief than to change a behaviour, and it’s especially true when the behaviour is something you’ve been doing for a decade and have perhaps spent thousands on.

The guy at my gym proudly wore his Rolex every day for over a decade, and I’d imagine he paid what was, to him, a hefty sum of money for this crowning achievement, so to speak. For him to admit that it may have a ‘humble’ aluminium bezel would be admitting he doesn’t know ‘his most prized possession’ as well as he believes he ought to know it... and I suppose that was too much dissonance to swallow at 7am on chest day.

I was probably wrong about how wrong people are

I actually learned a lot in this section. I started out assuming the backfire effect was a given - this is the idea that correcting someone’s false belief makes them believe the false thing more . A lot of research suggests this to be true and such theories have been repeated so often they have started to feel like common knowledge. Here’s another example in this 2010 paper by Brendan Nyhan and Jason Reifler ; they found that conservative respondents, when corrected on the Iraq WMD issue, doubled down instead of updating their views.

But what I learned was how this doesn’t always hold true.

A 2019 paper by Thomas Wood and Ethan Porter did five experiments across more than 10,000 participants on 52 politically charged topics. They only found the backfire effect in one of them - which happens to be the original WMD question from the Nyhan paper - and even then, this was only when they used Nyhan’s original wording exactly . All the other corrections, on every topic, seemed to push people toward the correct answer. 6 Nyhan himself has since done some follow-up work and slightly corrected his thoughts on the original findings as well.

So based on more current research, it seems people do generally update their beliefs when corrected. The issue is that they don’t bother updating their attitudes or identities nearly as much.

In my case, I can tell someone their bezel is aluminium, and maybe on some level they might eventually absorb it… but what they were really defending wasn’t even a bezel. If the guy was defending some version of himself who bought an unbeatable watch, that’s a much sadder thing to argue about than a bezel being ceramic.

There’s a specific type of online argument which will never be resolved. Someone posts a photo of a new purchase, say, a Cartier Santos. Within about 30 comments, several separate debates will be taking place concurrently.

One person is explaining that the Santos makes no sense because the resale value is poor compared to a Rolex. Another person is arguing that Cartier’s heritage in the Santos design purportedly predates almost everything else in modern watchmaking, so of course it makes sense. A third person is saying they’d never buy it because they tried one on and it just didn’t feel right on the wrist.

Clearly, these people aren’t even disagreeing with each other, they’re just answering different questions.

Estimated reading time: ~14 minutes

Another framework

Today we will explore a 1963 paper by Nikolaas Tinbergen - a Dutch ethologist who would go on to win the Nobel Prize for his work on animal behaviour. Tinbergen noticed that scientists studying animal behaviour kept talking past each other because they were using the word why to mean completely different things. His framework for sorting this out 1 turns out to be incredibly interesting when applied to watch collecting - and particularly good for understanding why collectors who seem perfectly intelligent can look at the same purchase and reach opposite conclusions.

Now, at the time, Tinbergen didn’t set out to create some sort of “universal theory of explanation” or anything; he was just trying to get his colleagues to stop arguing about things he saw they actually agreed on. Still, what he ended up with was a neat map of the different questions hiding inside “why did you do that?”

When someone asks why you bought a particular watch, they might be asking about your intentions (what were you trying to achieve?), or about your history as a collector (how did you end up valuing this type of thing?), or about what the behaviour accomplishes in some deeper sense (what is collecting even for?), or about how human beings ended up being the kind of creatures who collect things at all, or even about what was happening in your brain at the moment of purchase.

In fact, subconsciously, they may even be asking more than one of these questions at the same time, and your response will remind them about what remained unanswered (but post-fact). And sure, these are all valid questions, and some might even be interesting questions - but they have completely different answers.

Intent matters

I’ll start with the most obvious one, because this is the question people usually think they’re asking - it is about your intentions .

“I bought the Santos because I wanted something elegant that I could wear with a suit but also looked good with casual attire. I’ve always admired Cartier’s design language, and the price was right given my budget.”

This seems to be a perfectly reasonable answer. It explains your goals, your reasoning, your conscious decision-making process, and even your constraints. If you’re having a conversation with a friend about your new watch, this probably covers everything they might want to know.

Now, did you notice how this answer is silent on a bunch of other questions? It doesn’t explain why you have the aesthetic preferences you have. It doesn’t explain why humans collect things. It doesn’t explain what was happening neurologically when you handed over your credit card. It doesn’t explain why you didn’t just buy a Rolex, since Lotus will say you’re a moron for not doing so. Those are all different questions… valid, but different .

The thing about intentions is that they’re the one type of explanation that only works for the beings that actually have them. You can ask why I bought a Santos; you can’t meaningfully ask why the secondary market crashed in 2022 using intention-why, because markets don’t have intentions (some people talk as though they do, but that’s a different problem!).

Tinbergen actually excluded intentions from his original framework because he was studying animals and didn’t want to anthropomorphise 2 . Anyway, we’re discussing watch collectors, who definitely do have intentions - sometimes confused intentions, sometimes conflicting intentions, and oftentimes dumb intentions… but yeah, intentions nonetheless.

How did you get this way?

This all gets even more interesting when you think about the underlying developmental question - which is something like “ how did you become the kind of person who would make this purchase? ”

At first you might think wtf, that’s too deep - but it’s really not. Perhaps you grew up around someone who appreciated good design. Or maybe your first ‘real’ watch was a gift that steered your future taste. Maybe you spent years on forums absorbing particular aesthetic values or characteristics in a watch such as value retention . Or you may have had some formative experience - a trip to Geneva with a watch-nerd parent, a conversation with an inspiring watchmaker, or any similar moment when a penny dropped in your head.

The developmental answer to “why did you buy the Santos?” might be something like “ I spent my early collecting years obsessed with tool watches, but after a decade of that, I started noticing that what I actually reached for most often were thinner, more elegant pieces. The Santos represents where my taste has evolved to after 15 years of handling watches.”

This is a completely different type of answer than the intention answer from earlier. The intention answer is about your conscious goals at the moment of purchase . The developmental answer is about the long process that shaped those goals in the first place.

And yes, you might not even be aware of your developmental history. You might think you ‘naturally’ prefer elegant watches, without recognising all the experiences and exposures which created that preference. Some of the most interesting developmental explanations are probably ones you don’t know yourself - or at least, haven’t given much thought to.

Morgan Housel makes a similar point in his new book The Art of Spending Money 3 . There’s a saying inside the foster care system - “ All behaviour makes sense with enough information.” Once you understand what someone has dealt with in their life (be it uncertainty, formative experiences, little things which shaped their values) their behaviour begins to make sense. Housel talks about how this applies directly to the way in which people spend money; he says your spending habits reflect the social and psychological experiences of your life . Since those experiences vary dramatically from person to person, what makes sense to you might seem crazy to me, and vice versa.

A collector who grew up watching their father admire dress watches at a local retailer has a completely different developmental path to someone who discovered watches through seeing James Bond wearing a Rolex (or Omega) or Martin Sheen wearing a Seiko in Apocalypse Now! None of these is right or wrong… they just got here using different routes.

Wtf is happening inside your head?

This part is about the mechanism or what Tinbergen called “causation.”

When you walked into that boutique and tried on the Santos, something happened in your nervous system. Visual information was processed, reward circuits were activated (or not), memories were triggered, anticipation systems fired, and the physical sensation of the watch on your wrist was finally integrated into your existing expectations and preferences. It’s a lot of parallel processing, as you can imagine… and then, at some point during this parallel processing, you became committed to the purchase.

What actually happened in that moment?

Last year in Geneva Phillips sold a Prussian Blue Mirage 38 for CHF 241,300 and the watch was listed with an estimate of CHF 40-80k. I’d say the estimate was fair, given the retail price was around CHF 65k. In New York, a yellow gold Sienna sold for $190,500 .

As I type this, there is a Mirage 34 on Loupe This and bidding is at $262,000; Tony Traina wrote about this lot:

“A friend and I have the over/under at $329k—I took the over…”

Reminder: the retail on this 34 is CHF 58,500 excluding VAT right now, and that’s for a 2028 allocation. I believe these earlier ones were sold for ~CHF 54k.

Side note: I was editing the post after I wrote it yesterday… and here we are - it’s already blown past $350k and there are still 2 days remaining. At this rate we might be looking at $500k+.

As a result of this insane ‘performance’ … public chatter is going nuts; rigged allocation processes, brand-to-dealer-seeding to ‘pump the market’, manipulation by dealers, and what have you. I posted an IG story about this the other day… urging whiners to shut up. And I still maintain that position… I am not interested in Berneron as such; Journe is perhaps in the same boat, and so are Rexhep, Kari and several others. Give it a year or two, and there will be a new hype lord on the block.

What I want to focus on is the value gap; Berneron charged 65k for a watch, and then someone paid Phillips 241.3k for it - there’s a difference of CHF 176,300 here which might be fun to dissect.

Estimated reading time: ~ 13 minutes

Charge more?

I mean, sure, that seems obvious right? There is apparently demand at dizzying prices, so why is Berneron not raising the prices higher, and faster? You could argue that if the price is close to the current ‘market’ as shown by all the recent sales, historical auctions, and live auctions, then flipping will cease altogether. That’s logical, because there will be no ‘value gap’ to capture.

Well, get this: SJX actually asked Rexhep this exact question :

SJX: So now there was a gap between the retail price of RRCC and the recent auction value. So why don’t you increase the price?

RR: [laughs] I think this will be the choice of many people, but I have to come back to reality. I’m a watchmaker and we do it like this: you’re trying to calculate the cost, this your cost, and you’re trying to make some margin on it.

I want to stay like this. I am happy with what I am doing, so let’s keep it like this. I’m 36, so I should not be in a rush for anything. Fortunately today we don’t think about doing it just for money. It’s more about achieving something that I can be proud of.

So he’s saying he prefers cost-plus pricing 1 and despite being aware of the gap, he doesn’t want to pre-empt the market’s sentiment staying the same forever (i.e. prices stay elevated and hype stays strong). Prudent back then, and perhaps even more admirable that he continues roughly with the same philosophy today - given that in his case, the gap might stretch into the millions nowadays.

But ok, let’s do some calculations… and we will go with the lower price; $190,500 is about CHF 153k, and at a retail price of CHF 65k the gap is 88k. Apparently Berneron only made 24 of the planned Mirage 38 watches (his FAQ says he’s got a cap of 48 per reference per year), so let’s keep it conservative and use 24 for now. So, 24 watches at 65k is CHF 1.56m of revenue for the brand, but the same 24 watches with a CHF 88k gap is CHF 2.1m going somewhere else. 2

Point being, even with the most conservative estimate we have right now, Berneron’s watches make more money for other people than they do for the brand. Why on earth would anybody willingly run a business like that?

Why leave so much money on the table?

Check out this paper called “A Note on Restaurant Pricing and Other Examples of Social Influences on Price” - this is the abstract:

This note tries to explain why many successful restaurants, plays, sporting events, and other activities do not raise prices even with persistent excess demand. My approach assumes that demand by a typical consumer is positively related to quantities demanded by other consumers. This can explain not only the puzzle about prices but also why consumer demand is often fickle, why it is much easier to go from being "in" to being "out" than from "out" to "in," and why supply does not increase to reduce the excess demand.

This is basically the same concept we’re dealing with here… and I guess any regular SDC-reader will already know the outcome. Basically, for certain goods and services, a part of what people are buying is the fact that other people want it .

Which of course means if you raise the price and clear the queue, then you are destroying part of the underlying product which people are queuing to buy. If you have a half-empty restaurant with no queue, this is a worse situation than having a full restaurant with a long queue… even if the food is identical.

I already wrote about the loop this creates in the context of the scarcity/desire equation; but what we didn’t really cover is how to price this loop. I guess now we know… that CHF 176,300 premium someone paid at Phillips is basically a marketing fee. And you know what? I reckon it’s pretty good value.

Despite all its flaws, a public auction result will probably always be the best type of advertising available to a small independent brand. Berneron the company was founded only 4 years ago… and right now, the number of people who have never handled one but seem to know this name is kinda crazy. What would that have cost if he tried to buy that sort of awareness using his own marketing budget? A lot more than CHF 176,300 - that’s for damn sure.

—

Anyway. Aside from the marketing value of mega-hype premiums, there are actually some other good reasons why a brand can’t just raise the price.

I spoke about the axis recently; the basic premise there was that a brand is free to move up and down the ‘axis of its original promise’, but it can’t keep changing its promise. Take Rexhep’s promise (as per his quote above); he said openly that he wants to charge cost plus a fair margin. So if he suddenly charges prices which reach possible-auction-outcomes, this would be a direct communication to the world that he is now something different - which is actually a much harder sell than it seems.

Another reason is because prices are a ratchet; up might feel like it’s easy, but then going back down will feel like a catastrophe. If you keep hiking prices and then demand subsequently tanks, the psychological impact will be devastating to the brand.

Has anybody solved this?

Let’s turn to finance, as we often do around here; consider an initial public offering (where a company sells shares to the public for the first time). Typically there is an investment bank that ‘runs’ the IPO and for some massive IPOs there could be several banks. Anyway, the bank sets a price, and decides who gets to buy shares, and then manages this so-called allocation process. Just like watches! There’s a fixed supply of watches, and then there’s a set retail price, and in our case of hyped watches there are more buyers than watches… so someone makes a decision about who gets one and who doesn’t.

Now with an IPO, banks like to say they want long-term holders, and people who believe in the company and who might stick around through periods of volatility and so forth. Banks don’t want people to buy in and then dump the shares on the day the stock is trading on the open market.

—

In reality, though, even the banks can’t get this shit right. Check out this running dataset which evaluates American IPOs; on average, it looks like over nearly half a century, shares are worth 19% more by the end of the first day versus what the company sold them for. That’s an i-n-s-a-n-e amount of value ‘left on the table’.

So if some of the most sophisticated sellers and quants in the world are still leaving this much value on the table, I mean, Berneron and Rexhep and all the rest are seemingly in good company, no?

But wait, it gets even better!

With IPOs, there were scandals… and these scandals led to regulations. Specifically, we now have FINRA Rule 5131 which bans three things. First is spinning , which is offering allocations to the executives of companies whose banking business you want; so rewarding mates with hot allocations, basically. Next was quid pro quo allocations , which is giving or withholding shares in order to force excessive fees relative to the work done (basically using allocation as leverage, like force-selling a Gerald Charles to unlock a Daytona). And finally, recouping a salesperson’s commission when a client flips ; funny enough, they define flipping as selling the shares within 30 days.

Now if you try to transpose this to watches… spinning is the equivalent of a watch brand seeding a hype watch to his mates that are dealers to drive up the price. Quid pro quo I already shared the Daytona example. And the flipping rule works the same as any AD’s blacklist.

What’s funny is that all the whining in the world of watches is about well-documented failure modes which showed up ages ago in finance, and needed laws and regulation to stop it from happening. We have no hope, really, because even after all this regulation and red tape, the IPO still pops 19% on average.

So look, as far as I’m concerned, this isn’t solvable in the world of watches… this is just a set of trades, and watchmakers are picking theirs.

Why not just pick the right people?

A lot of people in our hobby suggest this as a solution… watchmakers and brand should ‘vet’ customers better… I think this is a useless and idiotic solution. If anything, it makes things worse .

Back to the Rexhep/SJX interview:

“We have this pressure. We want to have the right people – it’s long-term thinking for the brand.”

But how are you supposed to find these ‘right people’? I mean, it’s not like people turn up with a ‘love for watchmaking barometer’ on their forehead. Brands and watchmakers are forced to use proxies… what else do these people own, how often do they visit, what have they sold, can they describe what they love, who else can vouch for them, who are their friends, and so forth.

And while that’s all very interesting, this isn’t a real test of anything. To make any positive test result worthwhile, it needs to be difficult to pass . If it was easy to get into Imperial College or Oxford, then degrees from these universities would not be as highly regarded as they are. The problem with these so-called ‘tests’ for the proverbial ‘right people’ Rexhep mentions, is that they are easy to fake.

How can one fake being passionate about watches and watchmaking? Easy. It might take you about 300 hours over a couple of years. You can read a ton of stuff about watchmaking and the history of the craft, then you can go to all these events around the world, set up an IG account and consistently post and engage with the watchfam… next, you might need to buy a couple of decent watches and post about them, and you know, just be ‘visibly enthusiastic’ about it all. You might say, ‘fvck that, it’s a lot of effort, and I reckon most people wouldn’t bother’.

Well, you say that… but did you see the prize? For Berneron, remember the value gap was CHF 176,300 for a single watch. If it did indeed take 300 hours of your time, then this is nearly CHF 600 per hour you would be paid to become somewhat convincingly ‘interested in watchmaking’. If you used the premium on a Rexhep watch, I don’t even care to do the math but it’s roughly 5x more.

I know plenty of people would do this… I know because I know plenty of people who currently do this. So many of them are even more diligent about it than actual enthusiasts, because for them, it’s basically a type of job.

What this means, sadly, is that the test for passion actually gets weaker as the prize gets larger. Because think about it… when there’s no premium, only people who truly care will ever look at those watches. As soon as the premiums are hitting six figures, the ‘test’ will only measure ‘who is willing to invest in appearing to be passionate’ - which is of course, anyone who sees this as a way to make easy money.

But that’s not all… it gets worse than that.

You can spot a true believer, can’t you?

Ha! Who do you think looks most passionate to a watchmaker?

As my friend Doobooloo put it… the people who put a much larger proportion of what they’ve got into watches, come across as the most passionate. These are folks who talk about a movement for hours, and fly in for events, and show up with insane fervour every single time. When you compare these people to the rich folks who place orders via their PA, never come to dinners, spend less than 1% of their wealth on watches, and have never once had a discussion about anything technical… who do you think comes across as a ‘truly passionate’ collector?

Well, you know the answer, but this is the wrong answer for a watchmaker. It’s wrong because the person who was clearly stretching their own finances to scrape together 65k for a Berneron, will surely see 240k as ‘life changing money’. And therein lies the problem. These are the sorts of people who will see this gain and think about paying off a mortgage, and school fees, and other such ‘normal life’ problems. There is no version of this story where some guy can have a sensible conversation with their spouse and get away with telling them that their passion is more important than their real-world challenges.

But the other guy? The one who was too busy to come to dinners and chat shit? Well, they can afford to hold the thing for 30 years and leave it lying in a drawer somewhere. They don’t care, because it’s worth more to them to just say they have one.

All this means is this whole ‘passion screening’ process fails to keep flippers out based on passion, and what’s worse, it ends up hand-picking the exact people who are most likely to flip. It also works against the people who are least likely to flip, because they don’t seem passionate enough. As a watchmaker, you’re selling your life’s work, your passion, and so you’re tempted to reward devotion - but in reality, this can often end up being a signal of financial exposure. Not always, sure… but often enough.

So what could they actually do?

Rudy got deported back to Asia in 2020 and instead of disappearing into obscurity, he’s apparently thriving as what the article labels an ‘ outlaw celebrity ‘. Wealthy collectors in Asia are apparently hiring this guy to recreate impossibly rare wines i.e. the very thing that landed him in prison ! In other words, they actively want his cheap blends which purportedly taste identical to $10,000 bottles 1 .

The reaction from the establishment was, as you’d expect, pure rage. To quote Rudy’s lawyer:

“These wine snobs are offended by the fact that Rudy can do this. They are threatened by the concept that he can bring taste to a concept that they thought was only for them — like duplicating their $10,000 bottles for perhaps as little as a hundred bucks. Messing with very rich people’s hobby put Rudy in jail. Now he is using his skill in a way that will be beneficial for a larger segment of people in the wine market.”

Rudy’s crime was more than just the original deception, it seems. The worse offence, was making the inaccessible accessible, and proving that the emperor’s exclusive vintage was basically not exclusive at all, thanks to some clever chemistry.

—

Wine (and I suppose ‘taste’ in general) is just a series of chemical compounds which trigger your taste receptors in a particular way, and these send signals to your brain about how you experience or ‘taste’ the stuff in your mouth. Rudy proved that if you can reverse-engineer the formula, you can recreate an identical experience. Sure, you lose the provenance and story, but the liquid hitting your tongue can be identical, or close enough that it is indistinguishable.

When it comes to watches, it’s a little different; steel is steel, and gold is gold. A balance spring oscillating at 2 Hz does exactly what it does regardless of who assembled it. When someone like Philippe Dufour makes a Simplicity , and some hypothetical master watchmaker with identical skills makes something “materially indistinguishable”, what actually separates them? In reality, nothing material separates them at all.

For the sake of argument, assume that someone was able to make a Dufour Simplicity which used the same materials, had the same finishing quality, and was perhaps indistinguishable from an original version of the same watch made by the man himself. And let’s say this watch was gifted to you by some rich guy, and you wear what you believe is a genuine Simplicity for a couple of years.

You have no idea this isn’t made by Dufour, and you wear it to auctions, watch gatherings, and you even passed it around at a dinner where there were several other Simplicity pieces where everyone believed it was authentic. Then one day, you meet someone who also owns a Simplicity, and the serial number on your watches are identical. You’re both very alarmed, and send the watches to Dufour himself, hoping he can explain this situation.

Intro

Some of you may have come across me, A Watch Critic on Instagram ( @awatchcritic ). As the name implies, I enjoy giving criticism and debate around watches as ' nothing is perfect ' in my view. My Dutch roots have endowed me with a direct, no-nonsense perspective we Dutch are known/infamous for!

I collect with a 1 watch per brand philosophy, which broadens my horizon allowing me to appreciate a myriad of brands rather than fixating on just one. It also avoids strong bias in my collection and hopefully enforces my credibility as a critic, with a wide appreciation and understanding of what different brands offer. I do a lot of research on each brand before a purchase and around watchmaking in general, and have a professional interest and expertise in branding and consumer behaviour.

I see no need to play any of the typical AD games or have any particular loyalty to dealers or brands. And yes, every piece I own, no matter how cherished, isn't exempt from my scrutiny!

Fanboys, tribes & brand loyalty

The watch community, like many others, often falls prey to the allure of ' fitting in '. Many collectors feel compelled to own ' the basics '—a Seiko 5, G-Shock, Submariner, Speedmaster, or even a Patek. Without these, do you even ' belong '? So, what drives this need for validation?

My collection of over 30 watches, lacks all of these, but perhaps I just enjoy being different… Many enthusiasts are drawn to specific watch brands for a myriad of reasons. For some, it's a symbol of status or a reflection of personal significance. For others, it's a genuine belief in the superior craftsmanship of the timepiece.

Social status and watch collecting

Rolex, for instance, enjoys almost universal admiration or envy from most watch collectors (non-collectors may be more biased against what it represents). Its iconic status is undisputed, and its appeal spans both the casual wearer and the discerning collector.

Conversely, niche brands such as Grand Seiko cater more to the purists. These are the aficionados who are vocal about the unparalleled quality and craftsmanship they believe the brand offers, often asserting that it provides exceptional value for money at any opportunity they are given.

Both Rolex and Grand Seiko have cultivated a dedicated following. These aren't just casual admirers; they are fanboys in the truest sense. Passionate, loyal, and often fervent in their advocacy for their chosen brand, they congregate on dedicated forums, sharing insights, reviews, and experiences that often go beyond the watches themselves. Their discussions often transcend mere appreciation for the watches, delving into the history, mechanics, and nuances of each model.

This phenomenon isn't exclusive to the watch community. It's a manifestation of tribalism, a social construct that has been ingrained in human behaviour since the dawn of civilisation. Historically, humans have always sought to identify with groups that share our values, beliefs, or preferences. Our attire, our language, the symbols we adorn ourselves with including jewellery – these have always been markers of our affiliations and status in society.

In the context of horology, this tribal behaviour has evolved over time. As watch brands have developed their identities, narratives, and USPs, they've attracted specific segments of enthusiasts. These tribes, whether they rally around the utilitarian robustness of a Sinn or the artisanal precision of a Grand Seiko, are a testament to the powerful allure of branding and the deep human need to belong.

Watch Brands as Religions

Whilst my Instagram is strictly horology-centric, I can't help but notice the broader issues my Watchfam friends discuss and share, such as the Arab–Israeli conflict. With stories and posts from both sides of the conflict as the watch community in particular features many collectors and dealers from both religious backgrounds.

As an optimistic nihilist myself, I have no skin in the game and try to remain neutral and focused on what is objective truth and what goes against agreed social norms such as the killing of innocent civilians, which I obviously condemn entirely, regardless of the perpetrator. I try to listen to both sides and question information in an informed way. However, the media's biased portrayal of such issues is evident from both sides.

In DM’s with @kingflum about this subject he pointed out this notion of a ' party line ' that media, similar to politicians have to support. And how we can see something like this often happening in watch media that tend to support the party line, even when a controversial watch is released.

To me this raised the question: What are these 'parties' in watches?

Brands, from Swatch to Patek, from mainstream to independent, even fashion brands like Daniel Wellington, seem to operate very similar to religions or tribes, advertising their values, creating tribes (literally in the case of MB&F), loyalty and even with ADs serving as places of worship to these brands!

People seem to like equating watch brands to things like cars and other brands. That in turn got me wondering how much watch brands actually equate to religions.

Rolex and Christianity being the most obvious match to me, I decided to ask what ChatGPT (4) had to say…

ChatGPT Prompt: " I want to equate watch brands to religions, what watch brands would each major religion be and why? "

The results seemed very intuitive to me and the explanations quite insightful and funny:

I also asked it about some other religions/belief systems:

1. Agnostic:

- Agnosticism is about uncertainty or lack of commitment to a particular belief about the existence or non-existence of a deity. Their choice might be versatile and open-ended.

- Seiko: They offer a wide range of watches from quartz to mechanical, from dressy to sporty. Their vast variety can mirror the open-mindedness of an agnostic.

- Citizen Eco-Drive: It's reliable and doesn't commit solely to battery or mechanical operation, somewhat reflecting the middle-ground approach of agnosticism.

2. Satanist :

- Modern Satanism, especially as seen in the Church of Satan, is more about individualism, secularism, and skepticism rather than the worship of Satan. A watch that is bold, individualistic, or against the grain might appeal.

- Invicta : Known for bold and often oversized watches, this brand's audacity might align with the rebellious spirit of some forms of Satanism.

3. Atheist:

- Atheism is the rejection of belief in the existence of deities. An atheist's choice in watch would likely be based on personal aesthetics and functionality rather than spiritual or religious symbolism.

So there you have it, Invicta is the brand for Satanists , that explains a lot about their current lineup actually!

All jokes aside, there is a serious hate against some brands like Invicta and Hublot, that shows similarities to some religious hatred that is usually lacking much substantial basis or taken out of context such as price.

I will happily admit I bought a left-hand drive Invicta pilot chronograph watch (pictured) as a (much) younger man who couldn’t afford much more, alongside a Tissot Tank and ultrathin Swatch Skin which were a lot less impressive compared to the 46mm Invicta, but ultimately more in line with my current taste. But the fact Invicta made a left-hand drive watch made me feel it was for me, as a lefty myself.

I wore it proudly for a year or two and received many compliments as I was still in ignorant bliss about the crappy throw-away movement hiding inside and that big watches would soon go out of fashion! Did I perhaps buy this partly because I had an older cousin that had a Breitling and I wanted to belong to that tribe? This was the closest thing to a ‘ luxury ’ watch within my reach at that age. And did push my horology journey further.

So, where do you stand in this horological spectrum? Are you a staunch brand loyalist or a horological polytheist? While tribalism offers a sense of belonging, it's crucial to remain open-minded. Brands like Hublot or Daniel Wellington might be the antichrist to some, but is such disdain justified or merely a byproduct of popular tribalism? And are sole-brand collectors, in essence, horological zealots?

The watch media, with its brand affiliations and underlying agendas, often treads a fine line between advocacy and bias. As collectors, recognising and combating this inherent tribalism can pave the way for a harmonious watch community, where diverse tastes and critiques are celebrated and all brands respected. Let's strive for unity and shared love of watches that isn’t flamed by brand interests, ensuring that long standing ‘conflicts’ like Rolex vs Grand Seiko remain a thing of the past.

Anyone who has embraced the watch nerd label will, at some point, have read or participated in an online debate about watches . You can click that link and observe grown adults typing out dissertations, writing with the fervour of someone defending their country’s honour at the United Nations. One person will argue that Rolex’s Superlative Chronometer testing is superior to METAS certification, only for someone else to offer up a thousand-word rebuttal, with amplitude data no less. This is the psychological equivalent of two bald guys fighting over a comb.

Which made me wonder: why does anyone bother getting defensive over watches?

Estimated reading time: ~ 18 minutes

Pringles flavours

To understand the absurdity of watch forum warfare, I figured we could ‘start simple’ by thinking about how we handle normal differences in regular taste - and I mean taste quite literally here.

If your mate prefers Pringles BBQ crisps and you’re a salt-and-vinegar person, nobody loses sleep over it. You might give each other a bit of stick depending on who does the shopping for your road trip, but you basically just… move on. The human brain is actually very good at accepting such benign differences in preference. Neither choice is ‘right’ or ‘wrong,’ and both of you understand this instinctively.

When you scale that preference up the hierarchy of social, cultural, and financial investment, this is when tolerance goes out of the window. If you find yourself at Wolfgang Puck’s steak restaurant in Mayfair (very good btw), and order a steak well-done instead of medium-rare , I’m pretty sure everyone at the table will judge you… just like people will judge you if you turn up wearing a Hublot, well, anywhere. These are still just preferences - the same as Pringles - but they happen to carry ‘social weight’ now. What I mean by this, is that your choice becomes a proxy for your taste, your intelligence, and your identity.

In the world of watches, this dynamic reaches a fever pitch; a person might have a deep, inexplicable preference for an Omega over a Rolex (or the other way around), and the truth of the matter is that people simply like what they like. Attraction, be it in romantic love or indeed in watches, is inherently subjective… and yet, the debates are endless, sometimes vitriolic, but more often than not… fiercely defensive.

To understand this in more detail, we need to dig into how your brain makes choices.

By the way… the irony that I’m about to construct an elaborate (albeit research-backed) argument about why people construct elaborate arguments , is not lost on me 😂 - consider me Exhibit A if you must.

You decide before you start thinking

We all love to think of ourselves as highly rational connoisseurs. We might look at spec sheets, compare power reserves, examine finishing, determine what is ‘good value’, and then decide which watch is best for us... right?

Wrong.

Modern psychology has actually unraveled this assumption. Human beings operate on a principle that researchers call ‘affective primacy’ i.e. the emotional reaction to an object happens instantaneously, and often before your conscious mind has even started processing . Your preference for a particular brand is rarely the result of some dispassionate technical analysis and it almost certainly has roots buried far deeper than that. 1

A specific dial colour might trigger a subconscious memory of a formative childhood holiday. A particular brand might carry emotional weight because your father or grandfather wore one. A case shape might evoke something comforting that you can’t quite articulate. You simply ‘know’ you prefer one watch over another because you experience a kind of visceral sense of rightness when you look at it.

The problem is that we suffer from something which psychologists call the ‘introspection illusion.’ When someone asks you why you prefer a particular watch, you have no conscious ‘instant recall’ to the emotional or historical variables that actually shaped the preference you have today. You can’t say “Oh I bought this watch because its shade of blue reminds me of my favourite blanket as a child” because you don’t even know that’s the case. Your brain hasn’t given you access to that information explicitly .

So what are you supposed to do? You now have an explanatory void, and to fill this void (i.e. to maintain your self-concept as a rational decision-maker) you convince yourself that “logic” must be the answer… so you start talking about movements or whatever other sh1t you need to talk about, to convince yourself that you have rational beliefs. 2

Pivot to merit

Now let’s talk about post-hoc rationalisation - another well-documented psychological defence mechanism. The sequence is always the same, where you make a decision intuitively, and then you build a logical justification for it after the fact , both for your own peace of mind and to defend the choice against critics.

In the Rolex versus Omega context, this plays out fairly often, and you’ll recognise it immediately. The Omega person might aggressively assert that the Co-Axial escapement and METAS Master Chronometer certification render their watch anti-magnetic to 15,000 gauss, and that this stuff constitutes ‘objective superiority’. The Rolex person counters that Rolex’s Superlative Chronometer standard has stricter internal tolerances, that the movements are historically more reliable, and that 904L steel is better than 316L.

Both parties then plunge into highly specialised debates about isochronism and amplitude that neither is typically qualified to have. Or they may just turn to market prices and point out how the secondary market price ‘proves’ one is better than the other. The fatal flaw in all of it is that ‘better’ simply isn’t quantifiable here. Both watches tell time with a degree of mechanical accuracy that exceeds daily necessity, and neither is as accurate as a cheap quartz Casio. If one person just enjoys wearing the Omega more than the Rolex (or vice versa), the other person cannot possibly prove them wrong. In other words, this whole debate is just a performance, not a pursuit of truth.

What makes this insidious is a related phenomenon called choice-induced preference change (CIPC) . Decades of research findings have shown that people report significantly higher subjective valuations for items after having selected them. fMRI studies have revealed that this isn’t just ‘social performance’; the act of making a difficult decision triggers rapid emotion-regulation processes in the brain, and this literally alters how you encode subjective value - i.e. your brain rewrites its own assessment to justify what you already chose. 3

So when someone tells you that your watch is overpriced or technically inferior, your brain registers this as “someone poking a hole in a justification that your brain has worked very hard to construct” - it’s not just “someone challenging your preferences.”

With this reframing, it’s much easier to see why people can be triggered so easily.

By the way… none of this implies that technical differences don’t exist or don’t matter . A Co-Axial escapement is, objectively, an innovative achievement in watchmaking. Movement finishing does vary enormously across price points. Technical knowledge absolutely is valuable and worth developing. The underlying issue is not ‘the fact that people discuss technical merits’; the issue arises when technical arguments become a disguise for emotional preferences that the person can’t or won’t acknowledge. There’s a difference between “ I appreciate the innovation in a Co-Axial escapement ” and “ anyone who buys a Rolex over an Omega is dumb, because METAS .” The first is legit enthusiasm, and the second is your internal lawyer talking.

Your mind is a lawyer, not a judge
